summary: One of the documents that together define the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP). This one describes the abstract model: the printers, jobs, and operations that users and administrators can work with. It is a standards-track document. It was replaced by RFC 8011.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) gives programs a shared way to send documents to a printer over a network. This document defines the model behind it: what a printer and a print job are, the operations a client can ask for, and the attributes that carry the settings and the status. The encoding and transport of the messages are defined separately in RFC 2910.

questions: what is the internet printing protocol
what does ipp attribute fidelity do
subtitle: The model behind network printing: a Printer object, a Job object, the operations a client can request, and the attributes that describe them.

tldr.problem: Network printing needs a shared model that a client and a printer can both rely on, so that a client can submit a job, ask what a printer supports, and follow the progress of a job.
tldr.mechanism: IPP/1.1 defines two abstract objects, Printer and Job, a fixed set of synchronous request and response operations on them, and the attributes that describe capabilities, job settings and state. The encoding of those messages onto HTTP/1.1 is left to RFC 2910.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2911 was a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 2566 (IPP/1.0) and has since been obsoleted by RFC 8011, with RFC 3380, RFC 3382, RFC 3995, RFC 3996 and RFC 7472 updating it along the way.

today: RFC 2911 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8011, which is now the definition of the IPP/1.1 model, so this document is no longer current. It was also updated by RFC 3380, RFC 3382, RFC 3995, RFC 3996 and RFC 7472, and it had earlier obsoleted RFC 2566.

sections.title: The IPP Model and Its Document Set
sections.content:
The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) is an application-level protocol for distributed printing using Internet tools and technologies. RFC 2911 is the Model and Semantics document of IPP/1.1: it defines an abstract model of objects, their attributes and their operations that is independent of encoding and transport. RFC 2910 maps that model onto HTTP/1.1 and defines the application/ipp media type and the ipp URI scheme.

The model is deliberately simple. Real print systems are often multi-tier arrangements of end-user programs, print drivers, spoolers, print servers and output devices. IPP keeps that arrangement out of sight by exposing two object types, Printer (section 2.1) and Job (section 2.2). Each type has a set of operations (section 3) and a set of attributes (section 4).

The rest of IPP/1.1 lives in other documents: RFC 2567 sets out the design goals, RFC 2568 the rationale behind the model, RFC 2569 maps the Line Printer Daemon protocol onto IPP, and an Implementer's Guide gives practical advice on writing clients and IPP objects.
sections.plainLanguage: IPP gives programs a common way to send documents to a printer over a network. This document sets out what a printer and a print job are, and what a client can ask a printer to do. How the messages are written down and carried is defined in a separate document.

sections.title: Printer and Job Objects
sections.content:
A Printer object implements the server side of IPP/1.1. End users query its attributes and submit print jobs to it. What sits behind the abstraction can take several shapes: an output device with no spooling, an output device with a built-in spooler, or a print server with one or more output devices behind it. Because it is an abstraction, a Printer object could also stand for a fax device, an imager or even a CD writer.

A Job object models one print job. The Printer object creates it when it validates and accepts a create request. An implementation MUST support at least one document per Job and MAY support several. A document is either a stream of data in a format the Printer supports, typically a page description language, or a reference to such a stream. In IPP/1.1 a document is not an object: it has no identifier and no attributes of its own, and every processing instruction is a Job attribute that applies equally to all documents in the Job.

A Printer object contains zero or more Job objects, and a Job object is contained by exactly one Printer object. If the same document data is sent to a second Printer, a second Job object is created, almost identical to the first but with new identifiers. Both Printer and Job objects also have names, chosen by an administrator for a printer and optionally by the client for a job. A name need not be unique and only has local meaning.
sections.plainLanguage: IPP describes two kinds of thing: a printer and a print job. The printer accepts work and creates a job object for each submission. A job holds one or more documents, and the instructions that say how to print them belong to the job rather than to the documents.

sections.title: Identifying Printers and Jobs
sections.content:
Every Printer and Job object is identified by a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) so that it can be referenced persistently and unambiguously. The Printer's printer-uri-supported attribute holds one or more URIs. Two companion attributes have the same number of values: uri-security-supported names the security mechanism for each URI, such as tls or none, and uri-authentication-supported names the authentication mechanism, such as digest or none. A printer that offers both a secure and an open channel therefore has one URI for each channel.

When the client submits a job it names one of those URIs, and that URI MUST be one of the values in printer-uri-supported. The Printer then assigns the new Job a URI, stored in job-uri, and records the Printer URI that was used in job-printer-uri. The generated Job URI follows the security policy and the channel the client used, so a job that arrives over a secure channel gets a secure URI. The precise format of a Job URI is implementation dependent.

Many existing printing systems identify jobs only by a 32-bit positive integer, so the Printer MUST also generate a Job ID, stored in job-id. The Job ID is unique only within the Printer that created it. A client may therefore address a Job either by its Job URI or by the Printer URI together with the Job ID, and the implementation MUST support both forms. The two are not the same thing: names such as printer-name and job-name are for people, need not be unique, and have only local meaning.
sections.plainLanguage: Each printer has one or more addresses, which the RFC calls URIs, and a client uses one of them to reach it. The printer gives each new job an address of its own, plus a short number that is unique only inside that printer, so a client can name a job in either way.

sections.title: Requests, Responses and Their Common Rules
sections.content:
Every IPP operation is synchronous and consists of a request and a response. Every request carries a version-number, an operation-id and a request-id; every response carries a version-number, a status-code and the request-id of the request it answers. The client chooses the request ID, which MUST be an integer from 1 to 2**31 - 1, and the object copies all 32 bits of it into the response so that the client can match replies to outstanding requests. A request that ends before the whole request ID has arrived is rejected with a request ID of 0.

Requests and responses are built from groups of attributes: Operation Attributes, Job Template Attributes, Job Object Attributes, Printer Object Attributes, and the Unsupported Attributes group. Attributes within a group must be unique. Operation attributes describe the operation itself and do not outlast it; Job Template Attributes are the processing instructions a client supplies when it creates a job.

The order of the leading operation attributes is fixed. attributes-charset MUST be first and attributes-natural-language second, and the target attribute MUST be third, with job-id fourth when a Job operation uses the Printer URI plus Job ID form. All URIs in requests and responses must be absolute rather than relative.

Every response carries a status code, a number from 0x0000 to 0x7FFF. successful-ok means the operation worked. When the client supplies something the printer cannot use, the printer either rejects the request or carries on with substitutions, and it returns the offending attributes in the Unsupported Attributes group. That group covers three cases: an attribute the printer does not support at all, a supported attribute whose syntax or value is not supported, and supported values that conflict with one another.

Versions are not negotiated. If the major version in the request is not one the printer supports, the printer returns server-error-version-not-supported together with the closest version it does support. A minor version it does not recognise is normally accepted.
sections.plainLanguage: Each request names the operation and carries a number that lets the client match the reply to it. Every request and reply also says which character set and language its text uses, and which printer or job it is aimed at. When the printer cannot do exactly what was asked, it either refuses the request or prints the job with substitutions and reports which attributes it ignored.

sections.title: Submitting and Controlling Jobs
sections.content:
Three operations create a Job object. Print-Job sends the document data inside the request. It is a REQUIRED operation, so every implementation MUST support it, and it is the operation to use for a job with a single document. Print-URI sends only a URI and lets the printer fetch the document itself; if the printer does not support the URI scheme it MUST reject the request with client-error-uri-scheme-not-supported. Create-Job creates an empty Job that the client then fills with Send-Document or Send-URI operations, the last of which sets last-document to true. Create-Job is OPTIONAL, and a printer that supports it MUST also support Send-Document.

Checks happen at two different times. At job submission the printer validates the attributes, their syntaxes and their values against its own xxx-supported attributes, and it validates the syntax and the scheme of any supplied URI. It does not have to parse the document or follow the URI at that point, because those checks have to be made again when the job is processed. A client can also use Validate-Job to try the same attributes out without sending a document and without creating a job.

After the create request is accepted, the job is in pending, pending-held or processing. If the printer has no room it MAY reject the request with server-error-busy and close the connection before all the bytes have arrived, so a client must be ready to keep submitting. If an error turns up later, during processing, the printer can no longer change the status code it has already sent, so it records the problem in the job's job-state, job-state-reasons or job-state-message attributes for the next query to find.

Once a job exists, the client controls it with the Job operations: Cancel-Job and Get-Job-Attributes are REQUIRED, while Hold-Job, Release-Job and Restart-Job are OPTIONAL. Control of the printer as a whole comes from the OPTIONAL Pause-Printer, Resume-Printer and Purge-Jobs operations, which are meant for an operator or an administrator. Notification is out of scope: a client follows a job by polling.
sections.plainLanguage: A client submits a job either by sending the document with the request or by sending an address and letting the printer fetch the document itself. The printer checks which settings it can accept, accepts the job, and reports progress when the client asks. The client can cancel the job, hold it, release it or start it again, and an operator can pause or clear the whole printer.

sections.title: Attribute Syntaxes, Character Sets and Languages
sections.content:
Every attribute value has a syntax, and the syntax decides how the value is encoded and what it may contain. The basic syntaxes are text (a string of characters in at most 1023 octets), name (the same idea for user-friendly strings, in at most 255 octets), keyword (US-ASCII lowercase letters, digits, hyphen, dot and underscore, 1 to 255 characters), enum (an integer from 1 to 231 minus 1 with a keyword name), uri (at most 1023 octets), uriScheme, charset, naturalLanguage, mimeMediaType (at most 255 octets), octetString, boolean, integer (from -231 to 231 minus 1), rangeOfInteger, dateTime, resolution and 1setOf X. A few attributes accept more than one syntax, written in the RFC as type3 keyword | name, so that a site can add values of its own.

A response may carry an out-of-band value instead of a real one: unknown (the attribute is supported but the value is not known), unsupported (the attribute itself is not supported, and this value appears only in the Unsupported Attributes group) and no-value (the attribute is supported but the administrator has not configured a value). A client MUST NOT send out-of-band values in a request.

text and name each come in two forms. Without a language, the language is the one in the attributes-natural-language operation attribute. With a language, the value carries its own language tag, which overrides the operation attribute for that value alone. This is the Natural Language Override mechanism, and all clients and IPP objects MUST support it. The language part is limited to 63 octets.

All clients and IPP objects MUST support the utf-8 charset, and MAY support others that are registered with IANA. The attributes-charset value in a response MUST be the same as the one in the request; if the printer cannot use the charset the client asked for, it rejects the request, sets the response charset to utf-8 and returns client-error-charset-not-supported. The language in a response need not match the one in the request: the printer may answer in the language of the job or in its configured language and use the override mechanism for the values that differ.

A printer MUST accept any natural language the client supplies, whether or not it supports that language, and MUST remember it so that later queries report it. Only the messages the printer generates itself are limited to the languages listed in generated-natural-language-supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Each value has a type that says how it is written and how long it may be. Text values also carry their language, either for a whole request or for one value at a time. Every implementation must accept UTF-8 text, and must accept a language it does not know rather than reject the request.

sections.title: Job Template Attributes and Their Defaults
sections.content:
A Job Template attribute is a processing instruction the client may send when it creates a job, such as the number of copies, the media or the finishing. Support for them is OPTIONAL. If a printer supports an attribute called xxx, it MUST also support xxx-default and xxx-supported; if it does not support xxx, it MUST support neither, and it treats a client-supplied xxx as unsupported. A client can therefore ask the printer which values it accepts and which it uses when the client says nothing at all.

job-priority runs from 1 to 100, with 1 the lowest priority and 100 the highest. A printer that supports it MUST support the whole range, and it MUST print every job of priority n before any job of priority n-1. If the printer supports fewer levels than the range allows, it maps the value the client sent onto the nearest supported one using the formula roundToNearestInt((100x+50)/n).

The RFC's table pairs each Job Template attribute with the two Printer attributes that describe it. copies is an integer from 1 to MAX with a range of supported values; finishings is a set of enum values such as staple, punch or cover; page-ranges has no default but does have a supported-values attribute; number-up takes an integer or a range of integers; media and job-hold-until accept a keyword or a name so that a site can define its own values; orientation-requested and print-quality are enums. An attribute can be supported for one document format and not for another, for example orientation-requested for plain text but not for PostScript.

Section 15 of the RFC explains what happens when a Job Template attribute meets a job whose document data contains instructions of its own. The value of the IPP attribute SHOULD take precedence, and the REQUIRED pdl-override-supported attribute says whether the printer attempts that (attempted) or does not (not-attempted). Separately, ipp-attribute-fidelity decides whether the printer must reject a job whose settings it cannot honour (true) or may ignore or substitute them (false, which is the default). The RFC is explicit that fidelity governs whether the job is accepted at all, not whether instructions inside the document can be overridden.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the settings a client can send with a job, such as the number of copies or the paper size. For each one the printer supports, it publishes the list of values it accepts and the value it uses by default. A client can ask for that list first, so it never asks for something the printer cannot do.

sections.title: Job States, Reasons and Retention
sections.content:
job-state is a REQUIRED attribute with seven standard values: pending (3), a candidate to start but not yet processing; pending-held (4), not a candidate for a reason that is recorded in job-state-reasons, but it returns to pending when that reason goes away; processing (5), being interpreted, rendered or printed; processing-stopped (6), stopped for a reason and able to continue when it clears; canceled (7); aborted (8); and completed (9). The last three are terminal: the printer MUST reach one of them before it removes the job, and by then all of the job's status attributes have their final values.

job-state-reasons adds the detail. It MUST hold none when there is no reason. Other values name what is happening, such as job-incoming while the printer is still taking the document data, job-data-insufficient after a Create-Job, document-access-error when a document passed by reference cannot be fetched, processing-to-stop-point while a cancellation is under way, and job-restartable during the retention period. This attribute is meant to be extended: new reasons can be registered without disturbing clients that act on job-state alone.

The RFC divides a job's life into four phases. While a job is pending or processing it is not completed. When it reaches a terminal state the printer MAY keep it for a while with its document data, and that phase is called Job Retention; a client can use Restart-Job during it. After the retention period expires the printer deletes the document data and the job becomes part of the Job History. After a further implementation-defined time the job is removed, and Get-Job-Attributes and Get-Jobs can no longer say anything about it. Get-Jobs with which-jobs set to not-completed returns jobs in the first phase, and completed returns jobs in the second and third.

Restarting a job moves it back to pending or pending-held and starts it again on the same printer with the same attribute values. The progress attributes, such as job-impressions-completed, MUST be reset to 0, and the job keeps its job-uri and job-id. If any of the documents was passed by reference, the printer MUST fetch the data again.
sections.plainLanguage: A job moves through a small number of states, and the printer reports the one it is in and the reason for it. It waits, it prints, it can stop and carry on, and it ends as completed, canceled or aborted. When a job ends the printer may keep it for a while so that it can be printed again, and later it drops it from the list.

sections.title: Security Choices and Access Control
sections.content:
The RFC does not fix one security policy. It says IPP MUST be able to run with different security mechanisms and security policies, from very strong to very weak to none at all, because the risks depend on where the printer is and on what is being printed. Inside one organisation, over a private network, a site may decide that encrypting the document is unnecessary; over a public network the client may want the content protected in transit. The mechanisms themselves are defined in RFC 2910, and this document describes how they apply to the model.

Each URI of a Printer carries an authentication mechanism, taken from the values in uri-authentication-supported: none, requesting-user-name, basic, digest or certificate. The printer uses that mechanism to learn the name of the user making the request, the authenticated user. When a job is created, the printer stores that name in job-originating-user-name, and that user is the job owner. The requester must be the job owner, or an operator or administrator of the printer, to cancel, hold, release or restart a job, and must be an operator or administrator for Pause-Printer, Resume-Printer and Purge-Jobs. Otherwise the printer returns client-error-forbidden, client-error-not-authenticated or client-error-not-authorized.

Where more than one authentication mechanism is configured, the implementation needs a rule for deciding whether two authenticated names are the same user. One policy treats names authenticated by different mechanisms as different users, so a job submitted under a weak mechanism cannot be canceled under a strong one. Another policy accepts the later operation when its mechanism is not weaker than the one used to create the job, so a job submitted under requesting-user-name can be canceled under digest.

A printer may also hold attributes back. It may return fewer attributes than the client asked for, and it may return none of them, and the status code looks the same as when everything was returned. A client therefore cannot tell whether an attribute was present and withheld or was absent altogether.
sections.plainLanguage: The printer checks who is asking before it acts, using no check at all, the name the client claims, HTTP Basic, HTTP Digest, or a certificate. The user who submits a job owns it, and only that user, an operator or an administrator can cancel the job or pause the printer.

sections.title: Conformance Requirements and Extensions
sections.content:
A conforming client MUST support all REQUIRED operations and MUST supply attribute values that fit the syntaxes in this document. A conforming IPP object MUST implement the Printer and Job objects, MUST implement the REQUIRED operations, which are Print-Job, Validate-Job, Get-Printer-Attributes, Get-Jobs, Cancel-Job and Get-Job-Attributes, and MUST support the REQUIRED attributes, including all REQUIRED values for the attributes it supports. An IPP object MUST ignore operation attributes it does not know, but MUST reject a request that carries a supported attribute with an unsupported value. A client MUST handle a response that contains groups, attributes, values or status codes it did not expect.

Both sides MUST support the utf-8 charset. A client MUST support Client Authentication and SHOULD support Operation Privacy and Server Authentication; a Printer SHOULD contain support for both. Security MUST NOT be weakened when a client sends an older version number: a printer that enforces digest authentication for version 1.1 must do the same for a version 1.0 request.

The protocol is built to be extended. Section 6 defines how new keyword and enum values, attributes, attribute syntaxes, operations, attribute groups, status codes and out-of-band values are registered with IANA, and section 11 gives the formats for such proposals. Extensions registered this way are OPTIONAL for conformance, and a conforming implementation may return extensions the client does not recognise. Elements that are dropped from one version of the protocol are deprecated, so they can never be reused with a new meaning.

Appendix F lists the differences from IPP/1.0, the earlier model that this document obsoletes. Appendix E defines a generic schema for registering a printer in a directory service, so that clients can find printers by name, by organisational context or by filtered searches on their attribute values.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says exactly which parts an implementation must provide. It also leaves room to add new settings, operations and status codes later, and it describes how those additions are registered so that they cannot clash with what already exists.

viz.caption: THE GROUPS THAT MAKE UP A REQUEST OR A RESPONSE

root.label: One IPP request or response
root.note: Groups, in the order the RFC defines them

children.label: Document content, treated as a group for ordering

viz.caption: OPERATION IDS DEFINED BY THE RFC

items.label: Print-Job
items.desc: Submits one document, with the data in the request.

items.label: Print-URI
items.desc: Submits one document, with a URI the printer fetches.

items.label: Validate-Job
items.desc: Checks the settings without creating a job.

items.label: Create-Job
items.desc: Creates an empty job for later documents.

items.label: Send-Document
items.desc: Adds a document, with the data, to a job.

items.label: Send-URI
items.desc: Adds a document, by URI, to a job.

items.label: Cancel-Job
items.desc: Cancels a job that has not finished.

items.label: Get-Job-Attributes
items.desc: Reads the attributes of one job.

items.label: Get-Jobs
items.desc: Lists the jobs of a printer.

items.label: Get-Printer-Attributes
items.desc: Reads the attributes of a printer.

items.label: Hold-Job
items.desc: Keeps a pending job out of the schedule.

items.label: Release-Job
items.desc: Makes a held job a candidate again.

items.label: Resume-Printer
items.desc: Lets the printer schedule jobs again.

items.label: Purge-Jobs
items.desc: Removes every job from the printer.

viz.caption: ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT FROM THE RFC: SUBMIT A JOB, POLL IT, THEN CANCEL IT

messages.label: Print-Job
messages.note: The request carries the document data and the job settings.

messages.label: Response
messages.note: The status code, the job-uri and the job-id of the new job.

messages.label: Get-Job-Attributes
messages.note: The client asks for the current state of the job.

left.desc: The client sends the document data in the request.
